title: Sirocco Health - inference mode gating and burst readiness
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency SLOs for streaming chatbot and burst token spikes; discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, KV cache expectations, autoscale behavior, and an initial benchmarking plan. Agreed to run a token/sec streaming baseline and share security docs.
next_steps: Redwood to share hosted/dedicated performance spreadsheet and security pack
Sirocco to provide 2 representative prompt sets + traffic pattern (30s, 90s dialogs)
Schedule 2-hour benchmarking session week of Jan 27
action_items: Jordan Kim - send performance spreadsheet + pricing sheet by 2025-01-17
Priya Desai - prepare benchmark script template and test checklist by 2025-01-22
Marta Alvarez - upload anonymized prompt set and traffic trace by 2025-01-20
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. i'm jordan from redwood, i'm the ae for this region. with me is priya our solutions engineer.
[00:06] Lina Zhao: hey jordan, thanks. we want to be pretty frank about this — latency p95 is a blocker for our chat use case.
[00:12] Marta Alvarez: yes, our internal target is 300ms p95 for turn-taking in streaming mode, and we see token bursts up to 1200 tokens/sec during peak workflow.
[00:20] Jordan Kim: got it. 300ms p95 in streaming is tight. can i ask what model family and sequence lengths you're planning?
[00:27] Ethan Brooks: we're evaluating open-family models, 6B-ish for NLU and a heavier 13B for context summarization, typical generated chunks ~40-120 tokens, but sometimes long monologues hit 600 tokens.
[00:38] Priya Desai: ok, that helps. two axes to think about: model latency (per-token), and infra behavior under concurrent streams. streaming p95s are sensitive to token pacing and batching. are you more sensitive to cost or absolute latency?
[00:48] Lina Zhao: latency first. cost matters but we can justify reserved capacity if it buys consistent p95.
[00:54] Marta Alvarez: also data residency — some PHI touches, so private or VPC required for parts of the workload.
[01:02] Jordan Kim: understood. so we should consider a hybrid: private for PHI flows and hosted for lower-risk paths, or dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput. quick question — do you have a concurrency estimate? simultaneous user chats?
[01:12] Ethan Brooks: baseline 120 concurrent streams, burst up to 450 for 90–120 seconds during clinical batch-processing windows.
[01:22] Priya Desai: that's useful. with 120 steady-state streams, we usually size a dedicated pod set; bursts of 450 will need autoscale policies or burst capacity. key detail: are the streams long-lived (open websockets) or short-request/response?
[01:31] Marta Alvarez: websockets, yes. most are open sessions, keep-alive, we append user messages when they happen. about 70% of sessions are active at any time.
[01:40] Jordan Kim: ok websockets means KV cache reuse is very helpful — you'll get big wins from per-session KV persistence to avoid re-encoding context each time. we can pin sessions to nodes to keep kv locally warm.
[01:50] Ethan Brooks: how reliable is that pinning? we have multi-AZ failover requirements.
[01:55] Priya Desai: pinning is strategy-based. we do soft-affinity with automatic fallback: if a node goes down, the request will route to another node and we'll warm the cache, which causes a cold-start impact for the first few tokens. for critical flows you can enable cross-node kv replication but it increases network and memory cost.
[02:10] Marta Alvarez: hmm that cold-start spike is our worry — p95 could blow past 300ms if multiple sessions migrate simultaneously.
[02:16] Jordan Kim: yep. mitigation paths: 1) dedicated pools sized for expected failover; 2) shorter pin TTLs plus pre-warming script; 3) hybrid routing where PHI sessions are on private infra with more conservative failover.
[02:28] Lina Zhao: can you quantify the cold-start hit? ballpark numbers?
[02:32] Priya Desai: ballpark — for a 13B model on modern GPU, cold-start token latency might add 60–120ms for KV warm, sometimes more if quantization causes runtime memory moves. streaming p95 becomes model-dependent, but we often see p95 delta of ~1.3–1.8x for cold tokens. that is why autoscale and cache warmers matter.
[02:47] Ethan Brooks: we also saw previously when we burst requests concurrently token/sec measured to 1.2k, some endpoints queued and latency spiked nonlinearly. what does redwood do for queuing and overload?
[02:58] Jordan Kim: we have multi-tier routing — prefer local warm nodes, then dedicated fallback pool, then hosted lower-cost variants. for overload we can both queue (within short windows) and degrade to a smaller model variant. we try to avoid long queues by scaling buffer capacity.
[03:11] Marta Alvarez: tradeoffs there are tricky — model downgrade could affect output quality for clinical summaries. we need an SLO on quality too.
[03:17] Priya Desai: totally — that's why our rollouts use evaluation hooks to compare outputs for a subset of requests before full downgrade. for your case, we could set a canary rule that only downgrades non-PHI sessions first.
[03:28] Lina Zhao: on benchmarking — what data do you need from us to run a realistic streaming token/sec test?
[03:33] Jordan Kim: 1) representative prompt set, 2) traffic distribution (sessions/sec, tokens per second per session), 3) target p95 SLOs and cost envelope. ideally anonymized transcripts.
[03:44] Ethan Brooks: we'll get that. timeline? we want results within two weeks.
[03:49] Priya Desai: two weeks is reasonable for an initial baseline. we'll use our streaming harness to measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and observed queuing times.
[03:58] Marta Alvarez: one more — encryption at rest and KMS for model cache — we need to know if the cache can use customer-managed keys.
[04:05] Jordan Kim: yes, for private deployments we support customer KMS/HSM integration for keys; for dedicated we can integrate KMS with dedicated control plane. hosted also supports envelope encryption but with provider-managed keys by default — we can escalate to customer-managed under enterprise agreement.
[04:19] Lina Zhao: great. wondered about single-region vs multi-region failover. our users are mostly NA but we want fast fallback to EU nodes sometimes.
[04:26] Priya Desai: multi-region adds routing complexity. warm caches across regions are expensive; typical pattern is regional primary, remote failover to minimal capacity in secondary region, with fallback to lower-cost variants elsewhere.
[04:38] Ethan Brooks: i want to circle back to p95 math. if our target is 300ms, what headroom should we provision for KV warm and network jitter?
[04:45] Priya Desai: safe rule: provision for 50–80% headroom. so if nominal single-token latency is 180ms, you need to allow 120ms slack for cold/k-v and network. but we should run a profile — model choice and quantization change those numbers a lot.
[04:58] Jordan Kim: also consider batching policies — continuous batching improves throughput but increases token tail latency; streaming with small micro-batches gives lower latency at higher cost.
[05:07] Marta Alvarez: do you have a published benchmark for our model sizes? 6B vs 13B typical p95s in streaming?
[05:13] Jordan Kim: we have internal profiles; i will share a spreadsheet with per-model p50/p95 numbers across sequence lengths and GPU types — that will be in the performance pack.
[05:20] Lina Zhao: i remember seeing something about quantization profiles — does 4-bit quantization materially affect p95 variance?
[05:26] Priya Desai: 4-bit often reduces memory footprint and can improve throughput, but sometimes per-token latency increases slightly due to dequant steps. in practice quantization reduces cost dramatically and usually improves throughput under high concurrency; for tight latency p95s we test both.
[05:38] Ethan Brooks: ok, let's talk numbers for the benchmark plan. what do you propose as an initial test matrix?
[05:43] Priya Desai: initial matrix: 6B and 13B models; hosted baseline; dedicated with reserved pool; private VPC with KMS; sequence lengths 60, 200, 600; concurrency buckets 120, 300, 450; streaming vs non-streaming; measure p50/p95/p99, token/sec and cold-start penalty; run 20-minute sustained windows and 2-minute burst windows.
[06:05] Marta Alvarez: sounds thorough. will you simulate our websocket patterns or should we provide a trace?
[06:10] Jordan Kim: best is to provide your trace; if not, we'll synthesize similar.
[06:14] Lina Zhao: one operational question — how are alerts surfaced when p95 degrades?
[06:19] Priya Desai: in console we have model-route dashboards, you can set alerting on p95 levels, token/sec, error rates, and fallback counts. alerts integrate with pagerduty/slack.
[06:27] Ethan Brooks: do you record audit logs for inference requests for compliance? we need an audit trail for PHI processing.
[06:33] Jordan Kim: yes, private and dedicated have full audit logs; hosted has request-level metadata retention options you can enable. we also support SSO/SAML and role-based access control.
[06:42] Marta Alvarez: great. we're also evaluating an in-house runtime but it's a maintenance burden. what's the uplift to migrate if we start with hosted and later move to private?
[06:51] Priya Desai: our deployment abstraction means the API surface is the same; migrating state (like KV caches) is workload-dependent. we provide migration assistance and data import tooling. many customers start hosted, then move critical flows to private.
[07:02] Lina Zhao: ok next steps recap?
[07:05] Jordan Kim: we'll send the performance pack and an initial benchmark script. you will send the anonymized prompt sets and the traffic trace. schedule a two-hour benchmarking workshop week of Jan 27.
[07:14] Marta Alvarez: agreed. Jordan, can you also include cost estimates for reserved capacity sized for 450 burst headroom?
[07:20] Jordan Kim: yes, we'll include that in the spreadsheet.
[07:24] Ethan Brooks: and include notes on KV replication options and estimated added memory/network overhead.
[07:29] Priya Desai: will do.
[07:31] Lina Zhao: thanks all. any closing thoughts?
[07:34] Jordan Kim: thanks everyone — expect the pack by Jan 17. we'll put a calendar hold for benchmarking week; feel free to adjust.
[07:41] Marta Alvarez: thanks, bye.
[07:43] [call ended]
